metadata.title: PISA 2018 Results (Volume I): What Students Know and Can Do

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA volume reports results based on the PISA 2018 international assessment design, which uses complex sampling to obtain representative samples of 15-year-olds within participating education systems. The publication notes that when school principal responses are presented, they are weighted so that they are proportionate to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in the school, indicating the use of weighting for school-level reporting. For student-level achievement reporting, the report relies on OECD/PISA scaling and reporting procedures that are designed to support population-representative estimates across countries and economies, but the specific student weight variable names are not provided in the excerpt. Because this is a framework/report-style publication rather than an ML re-analysis paper, the manuscript does not specify whether analysts should apply particular student weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or replicate weights; users should follow the PISA 2018 technical documentation for the correct weight and variance estimation variables.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This volume is a descriptive large-scale assessment results report rather than an empirical predictive analysis paper that specifies a plausible-values (PV) workflow for a model-based outcome. The excerpt describes PISA score reporting and missing-data symbols (e.g., 'm', 'c', 'a', 'w', 'x') but does not document an analysis-specific PV combining or missing-data imputation/deletion strategy. Therefore, PV handling and missing-data handling are not reported at the level required for an ML-methods extraction.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The excerpt states that 600,000 students representing about 32 million 15-year-olds in the schools of 79 participating countries and economies sat the 2-hour PISA test in 2018. It also specifies the PISA target population as 15-year-olds aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months who are enrolled in school and have completed at least 6 years of formal schooling, regardless of institution type, and it notes that PISA uses exclusions and response-rate procedures (with an overall exclusion rate figure referenced). No additional analytic subsample restrictions (e.g., specific grade bands, subject-only subsamples, or task-completion filters) are described in the provided text; therefore, the analytic sample is treated as the full available PISA 2018 target population for the reported comparisons.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA 2018 Results (Volume I) report summarizes how 15-year-olds performed in reading (main subject), with mathematics and science also reported, across 79 participating countries and economies. The reading assessment was delivered on computer in most participating systems and was designed to measure reading literacy in a digital environment while maintaining trend comparability over the past two decades. Results are reported using proficiency levels (e.g., Level 2+ and Level 5/6) and mean scores on the PISA scale, with statistical significance assessed at the 5% level. The report also provides context on coverage (15-year-olds in school), and it uses standardized missing-data symbols (e.g., 'm', 'c', 'a', 'w', 'x') to denote why some indicators are not available or not applicable. While the excerpt includes many substantive findings (e.g., top performers and shares at proficiency levels), it does not present an ML modeling pipeline or predictive metrics, so no ML-specific methodological extraction is applicable.
